title: Pilot
note: Episode 1, rebuilt teaching-first from storyboard/pilot.html: the map of a web app, one search through it, then four decisions checked against Thursday's requirements. Played by scenes/pilot.gd. Hours, prices and counts are illustrative.

lines.say: Welcome to the house. Ten percent of whatever you make under this roof is mine. In return, I make you a founder. There's no paperwork. There's a little paperwork.
That's Aleister Jr. It runs on Aleister, my server in the garage. It writes code all night and it has never once asked a question.
... Two hundred thousand. On Thursday, two hundred of my diners try Forkcast. On whatever they carry.
Some have iPhones, some have Android phones, some will be at their desks on laptops. If they can all use it and it finds them a table, he invests.
Eight hours! I know exactly what to build. I'll start now!
Before it builds anything: the whiteboard. There are decisions here we can't take back on Friday.

goal_card.head: THURSDAY: WALTER'S TEST
items: 200 diners, on iPhones, Android phones and laptops
Each asks for an evening and gets a place that fits

map.prompt: Ricky's whiteboard · every web app, drawn four ways · tap each box

hint.say: Every app you'll ever build is some version of this. Four boxes. Tap each one.

map.done: next: follow one search through it

device.h: The frontend: the diner's phone or laptop
device.pic: The dining room. What the diner sees and touches.
device.real: Frontend, or the client. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a browser; or an app.
device.fk: The search box, the answers, the Book button.
device.note: It runs on their device, not ours.

server.pic: The kitchen and the front desk. Diners never go in.
server.real: Backend, or the server. Code on a computer we run or rent.
server.fk: Checks each search, applies the rules, calls the AI model.
server.note: Only we can change what it does.

db.pic: The reservations book. Written down, kept for good.
db.note: The server reads and writes it; diners never touch it directly.

model.pic: An expert we phone. We pay for every call.
model.real: A model's API: the menu of requests another company's servers accept.
model.fk: Turns "quiet for six on Friday" into suggestions.
model.note: We call it with a secret key that proves the bill is ours.

list.t: Walter types “quiet for six, Friday” and taps Search. The frontend packs it into a request.
list.eg: { "party": 6, "night": "Friday", "quiet": true }  is JSON: a filled-in form

list.t: It crosses the internet to forkcast.app. DNS turns that name into the server's address. HTTPS seals it, so nobody on the café Wi-Fi can read it.
list.eg: The phone book, and a sealed envelope.

list.t: The backend checks it's a real request, then calls the AI model's API with our secret key.
list.eg: The kitchen decides; the dining room only asks.

list.t: The model suggests five places. We pay a little for this call.
list.eg: About a cent or two a search. Illustrative, like all the game's prices.

list.t: The backend asks the database which of the five have a table for six on Friday, then saves Walter's request.
list.eg: Kept for good: the server can restart, the request is still there.

list.t: The response comes back, and the frontend draws the answer: Nonna's back room. All of that took about a second.
list.eg: Every tap that fetches something is one trip round this loop.

lines.say: Three apps! iPhone in Swift, Android in Kotlin, and one for laptops. Native, like the real companies!
Native is where the serious developers are. Nobody's impressed by a website.
Three apps is three sets of bugs, and every fix queues for two app stores.
Nobody types a web address any more. If it isn't in the App Store, it isn't a real company.
Tap each one. They're all real choices. The question is which one fits Thursday.

hint.say: Tap each way to see what it's good at and what it costs.

platforms.rn: In the browser · e.g. Next.js, React
platforms.how: One site that opens from a link in any browser, laid out for phones first.
platforms.good: Every device from day one. A fix reaches everyone on their next tap.
platforms.cost: Fewer phone powers. Not in the app stores.

fix: Change the site and every diner has the fix on their next tap.
remind: Works on Android. On iPhone only once it's added to the home screen.

platforms.how: The same web app, which diners can also add to their home screen like an app.
platforms.good: Everything the web app does, plus an icon and notifications once installed.
platforms.cost: Still not in the stores. iPhone notifications need it on the home screen.

link: The link opens it; installing is optional.
remind: Once it's on the home screen, iPhones included.

platforms.rn: Swift for iPhone · Kotlin for Android
platforms.how: A separate app for each kind of phone, from the App Store and Google Play.
platforms.good: The smoothest feel, and every phone feature: camera, background location, widgets.
platforms.cost: Two codebases, three with laptops. Every update waits for store review, then for each person to update.

all: Laptops would need a third app.
time: About 20 hours for the two phone apps.
link: Testers install a test app first, then ours.
fix: Each fix waits for store review, usually about a day, then for every person to update.

platforms.how: One codebase that becomes both an iPhone app and an Android app.
platforms.good: One codebase for both phones, close to the native feel.
platforms.cost: Still goes through both stores. Laptops need a separate web version.

all: Both phones from one codebase; laptops need a web version too.
time: About 12 hours, before any web version.
fix: Most fixes go through store review; some tools can send small fixes straight to phones.

pick.prompt: Decision 1 · Pick one, and check it against Thursday
pick.head: The four ways

reqs.t: Works on iPhones, Android phones and laptops
Built in the 8 hours, with time left for the rest
Opens from the link in Walter's email
A fix on the night reaches everyone in minutes

native.say: A real company! I'll tell the press.

cross.say: One codebase, two stores. That's the grown-up answer.

pick.wrong: Right for another product: one that lives on the phone, uses the camera or background location, or wants a place in the stores. Wrong for Thursday.
pick.right_head: What to tell your AI: “a responsive web app, mobile first.”
pick.right: Start on the web unless there's a reason not to. Make it installable when reminders matter; go native when the phone itself is the product.

lines.say: Good news: we don't need a server at all! The app talks straight to the AI model. Fewer boxes. Simplest possible!
Let me look at the app.

noserver.button: Open the app's code, as any browser can
code: // app.js · downloaded by every diner's browser

after.say: That's our key. Every diner downloads it with the app. Anyone can copy it and run their own projects on our bill.
The phone can't keep a secret. That's what the box in the middle is for.

stamp.label: THE RULE
stamp.plain: Everything sent to a browser or a phone can be read and changed by whoever holds it. Secrets and rules stay on the server.
stamp.eg: Real term: a secret key (or API key). What to tell your AI: “keep keys on the server.”

sort.prompt: Decision 2 · What goes where? Tap a piece, then where it lives
sort.done: Screens on the phone, rules and secrets on the server, what must last in the database.
sort.take_back: Tap the red one to take it back and move it.

why.front: What diners touch has to be on their screen.
why.back: The server can send it, but it runs on the diner's screen.
why.db: A database stores data, not screens.

why.front: What the screen remembers right now. Real term: state.
why.back: Asking the server on every tap is slow. Keep it on the screen until they press Search.
why.db: Nobody needs it once they press Search.

why.front: Anyone can open the app and copy it. Gilroy just did.
why.back: Only our server uses it, read from its settings.
why.db: It isn't data the app looks up. It goes in the server's settings.

why.front: A diner can edit the page and pay $0.
why.back: The server works out the price; the phone only shows it.
why.db: The price can be stored here, but the server has to be what applies it.

why.front: Hiding a button keeps nobody out. They can ask the server directly.
why.back: The server checks every request. Real term: authorization.
why.db: The database holds bookings; the server decides who sees them.

why.front: Each phone would know only its own, and lose them with the phone.
why.back: In the server's memory they vanish when it restarts.

why.front: Too big for every phone, and out of date by tomorrow.
why.back: The server reads them from the database when it needs them.
why.db: One copy, kept up to date.

zones.s: Backend · only we can change it

backend.prompt: Decision 3 · Build the backend, or rent it?

options.rn: e.g. Node.js with TypeScript, on a server
options.good: Full control: any rule we can describe.
options.cost: We look after logins, backups and updates ourselves.

save: In a database we set up.

options.good: Database, logins and file storage ready-made; small server functions for our own rules.
options.cost: Its way of doing things, some lock-in, and a bill that grows with us.

later: Possible; big integrations may need our own server later.
take: Supabase is Postgres, which moves; Firebase's database is its own format, harder to leave.

options.n: An AI app builder makes and hosts the lot
options.good: The fastest start: describe it and it's live.
options.cost: Hard to change how it works underneath. The app lives on their platform.

rules: As far as the builder allows.
later: Custom connections are where these struggle.
take: Many export the code, but it's built their way.

reqs.t: Keeps every diner's request for good
Our own rules run on a server (the fee, who sees what)
Can talk to restaurants' booking systems
We can take it with us if we outgrow it

quip.say: Renting is someone else's server with a nicer website. Sometimes that's exactly what you want.

backend.wrong: None of these is wrong forever. Many teams rent first and build their own pieces as they grow.
backend.right: Renting is faster and costs control; lock-in is how hard it is to move out later. Tell your AI: “Supabase for the database and logins; our rules in server functions.”

plan.prompt: Decision 4 · Aleister's plan. Tap each line to place it
plan.head: FORKCAST · TECH STACK

c.pwa: Frontend: Next.js (React + TypeScript), mobile first, installable

plain.web: Next.js is a popular framework for web apps. React draws the screens; TypeScript catches some mistakes before anything runs. Mobile first: decision 1.
plain.pwa: Next.js is a popular framework for web apps. React draws the screens; TypeScript catches some mistakes before anything runs. Mobile first and installable: decision 1.

lines.c: Backend: Next.js API routes, hosted on Vercel
lines.plain: Small pieces of server code in the same project, run by a host called Vercel only when a request arrives. Real term: serverless.
The rented backend from decision 3. Postgres is the database underneath, the most common one there is.

lines.c: AI: model API, called from the backend only
lines.plain: Searches go from the phone to our server, then to the model, as on the whiteboard. Decision 2.
An environment variable: a setting kept outside the code. But in Next.js a name starting NEXT_PUBLIC_ means “include this in what every browser downloads”. The key is headed for the phone again.

intro.say: Here's the plan! Every line is a choice you made. Mostly.

plan.fix_button: Tell Aleister: the key stays on the server

fixed.say: Fixed! I named it public because... I see it now.

stamp.label: NEW WORD
stamp.plain: The list of tools a plan uses, layer by layer. Before you merge, put every line on the map. A line you can't place is a question to ask.

cheque.say: Walter's cheque. Two hundred thousand. He wrote one word on the back: “Boring.” From Walter, that's a compliment.

postmortem.runway: Walter's $200,000, and $15,000 a month to run the house. From next episode, every box costs some of it.

live: Live: under 9 in 10 found a place
lean: Lean: built only what Thursday needed
Lean: an hour on reminders Thursday didn't need
ulrich: Ulrich: picked native apps, for show

lines.say: Forkcast is a beautiful idea. Hubbub would like to give it a home. Four million dollars, today.
Why pay four million for something he could build in a month? Unless he wants nobody to build it.
... My two hundred thousand stands. One question. Where do people sign up?
A page for people to sign up on. By Saturday, for Ulrich's party. I'm going to be sick.
